originalTitle: The Market Looks Expensive. This ETF Pays a 11.86% Yield While You Wait for It to Come Down
summary: With the S&P 500 trading at stretched valuations, one lesser-known ETF takes a completely different approach to generating income, one that doesn't depend on stocks continuing to climb.
content:
With the S&P 500 trading at stretched valuations, one lesser-known ETF takes a completely different approach to generating income, one that doesn't depend on stocks continuing to climb.

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

I’m not particularly enthusiastic about buying the U.S. stock market at today’s valuations. As of Sept. 21, the S&P 500’s trailing price-to-earnings ratio was estimated at 26.48, while the cyclically adjusted Shiller P/E was around 41. Those aren’t timing signals, and expensive markets can remain expensive for years, but both measures suggest investors are paying a substantial price for current and normalized earnings.

The usual response is to look somewhere else. You could tilt toward value or smaller companies, increase international exposure, or simply sit on more cash and Treasury bills. None is necessarily a perfect solution. Factor tilts can underperform for years, international stocks introduce their own risks, and cash can leave you sitting on the sidelines if expensive U.S. stocks keep climbing.

There’s another approach I find interesting for investors who want to remain invested while getting paid to wait: options income. Rather than relying entirely on stock prices moving higher from already elevated valuations, an options strategy can monetize volatility and generate returns when markets move sideways.

One of the more unusual implementations I’ve found is the Peerless Options Wheel Income ETF (WEEL) . It currently has a distribution rate around 12%, but unlike many high-yield options ETFs, it isn’t simply writing covered calls against the S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100.

How WEEL’s Options Wheel Works

WEEL uses what’s commonly known as the wheel strategy, primarily through highly liquid sector ETFs rather than individual stocks. You can find investors using variants of this approach on communities like Reddit’s r/thetagang.

The first part involves selling out-of-the-money cash-secured puts. A put seller collects an upfront premium in exchange for agreeing to buy the underlying ETF at the strike price if it’s assigned. WEEL holds Treasury bills as collateral, so the cash securing those puts can continue earning short-term interest while the fund collects option premiums.

If the underlying ETF stays above the strike, the put expires and WEEL keeps the premium. The process can then begin again. If the price falls sufficiently and the position is assigned, WEEL takes ownership of the underlying ETF. It can then move to the second half of the wheel by selling covered calls against that position, collecting additional option premium until assignment.

The fund can rotate among different market segments depending on where its managers see attractive opportunities. Its recent exposures have included areas such as software, emerging markets, oil services, biotech, gold miners, silver and volatility-related strategies.

That’s one reason I find the strategy more interesting in an expensive market. WEEL doesn’t require the S&P 500 to keep marching higher to generate cash flow. Put premiums, covered-call premiums and interest earned on Treasury collateral can all contribute to returns.

There is plenty of risk involved. Selling puts means getting paid to assume downside risk. A severe selloff can leave the fund owning assets well above their prevailing market prices. Covered calls can subsequently limit the recovery if those positions rebound quickly. A 11.86% distribution should therefore be viewed as compensation for taking several risks.

WEEL’s Track Record Is Getting Interesting

The encouraging part is that WEEL’s high distribution hasn’t come at the expense of total return so far. I ran WEEL against the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPI) using Testfolio from May 16, 2024 through Sept. 21, 2026, giving us approximately 2.35 years of comparable history.

Over that period, WEEL produced a 33.33% cumulative total return, equivalent to a 13.03% compound annual growth rate. JEPI returned 19.31% cumulatively, or 7.81% annualized. WEEL accomplished that with higher volatility, at 12.47% versus 10.72% for JEPI. Its maximum drawdown was also deeper at 17.43%, compared with 13.26% for JEPI. But the additional risk has been compensated so far. WEEL posted a 0.72 Sharpe ratio versus 0.37 for JEPI.

That’s important because I don’t judge an income ETF primarily by its distribution rate. If a fund pays 11.86% while continually losing NAV, the headline yield isn’t telling you much about what you’re actually earning. WEEL’s 33.33% cumulative total return suggests that, over this particular period, the strategy has generated economic returns.

The drawback is cost. WEEL’s gross expense ratio is 1.24%, including acquired fund fees and expenses, with a 0.25% contractual fee waiver bringing its current net expense ratio to 0.99%. That’s expensive compared with a conventional index ETF.

There’s also no guarantee its recent performance persists. The wheel tends to benefit from markets where option premiums are sufficiently rich and underlying assets don’t suffer prolonged collapses. A powerful bull market can also leave an options-selling strategy behind because repeatedly monetizing volatility means surrendering some upside.

For me, that’s the trade-off. If I thought U.S. stocks were cheap and positioned for another sustained expansion in valuation multiples, I’d rather own them outright through a low-cost index ETF. At today’s valuations, however, I can see the appeal of sacrificing some potential upside in exchange for a hefty distribution.

chineseTitle: 市场看起来很贵。当你等待它下跌时，这只 ETF 的收益率为 11.86%
chineseSummary: 由于标准普尔 500 指数的估值过高，一只不太知名的 ETF 采用了一种完全不同的方法来产生收入，这种方法不依赖于股票的持续上涨。
chineseContent:
由于标准普尔 500 指数的估值过高，一只不太知名的 ETF 采用了一种完全不同的方法来产生收入，这种方法不依赖于股票的持续上涨。

这篇文章可能包含来自我们的赞助商和附属机构的链接，Flywheel Publishing 可能会因通过他们采取的行动而获得补偿。

我并不是特别热衷于以今天的估值购买美国股市。截至 9 月 21 日，标准普尔 500 指数的往绩市盈率为 26.48，而周期性调整的希勒市盈率约为 41。这些都不是时机信号，昂贵的市场可能会在未来几年内保持昂贵，但这两项指标都表明投资者正在为当前和正常化收益付出高昂的代价。

通常的反应是寻找其他地方。你可以转向价值公司或规模较小的公司，增加国际风险敞口，或者干脆持有更多现金和国库券。没有一个解决方案一定是完美的。因素倾斜可能会在多年内表现不佳，国际股票也会带来自身的风险，如果昂贵的美国股票继续攀升，现金可能会让你处于观望状态。

我发现还有另一种方法对于那些希望在等待报酬的同时继续投资的投资者来说很有趣：期权收入。期权策略不是完全依赖股价从已经较高的估值中走高，而是可以将波动性货币化，并在市场横向波动时产生回报。

我发现的最不寻常的实现之一是 Peerless Options Wheel Income ETF (WEEL)。它目前的分配率约为 12%，但与许多高收益期权 ETF 不同，它并不是简单地针对 S&P 500 或 Nasdaq-100 进行备兑看涨期权。

WEEL 的期权轮如何运作

WEEL 采用通常所说的轮盘策略，主要通过高流动性的行业 ETF 而不是个股。您可以在 Reddit 的 r/thetagang 等社区中找到使用这种方法变体的投资者。

第一部分涉及出售价外现金担保看跌期权。看跌期权卖方收取预付款，以换取同意以执行价格购买标的 ETF（如果已分配）。 WEEL 持有国库券作为抵押品，因此保证这些看跌期权的现金可以继续赚取短期利息，同时基金收取期权费。

如果标的 ETF 保持在行使价之上，则看跌期权到期，WEEL 保留权利金。然后该过程可以再次开始。如果价格充分下跌并且头寸被分配，WEEL 将获得基础 ETF 的所有权。然后，它可以通过出售该头寸的备兑看涨期权来进入轮盘的后半部分，在分配之前收取额外的期权费。

该基金可以根据其经理在哪些细分市场看到有吸引力的机会而在不同的细分市场之间轮换。其最近的风险敞口包括软件、新兴市场、石油服务、生物技术、金矿、白银和波动性相关策略等领域。

这就是我发现该策略在昂贵的市场中更有趣的原因之一。 WEEL 并不要求标准普尔 500 指数持续走高以产生现金流。看跌期权费、备兑看涨期权费和国债抵押品赚取的利息都可以贡献回报。

这其中存在很多风险。卖出看跌期权意味着获得报酬以承担下行风险。严重的抛售可能会使基金拥有的资产远高于现行市场价格。如果这些头寸迅速反弹，持保看涨期权随后可能会限制复苏。因此，11.86% 的分配应被视为对承担多种风险的补偿。

WEEL 的业绩记录变得有趣

令人鼓舞的是，到目前为止，WEEL 的高分配并没有以牺牲总回报为代价。我从 2024 年 5 月 16 日到 2026 年 9 月 21 日使用 Testfolio 对摩根大通股票溢价收入 ETF (JEPI) 进行了 WEEL 对比，得到了大约 2.35 年的可比历史。

在此期间，WEEL 产生了 33.33% 的累计总回报率，相当于 13.03% 的复合年增长率。 JEPI累计回报率为19.31%，年化回报率为7.81%。 WEEL 实现了这一目标，但波动性更高，为 12.47%，而 JEPI 为 10.72%。其最大回撤也更深，为 17.43%，而 JEPI 为 13.26%。但到目前为止，额外的风险已经得到补偿。 WEEL 的夏普比率为 0.72，而 JEPI 的夏普比率为 0.37。

这很重要，因为我主要不是通过分配率来判断收益 ETF。如果一只基金支付 11.86% 的利率，但资产净值却不断损失，那么总体收益率并不能告诉你多少实际收益。 WEEL 33.33% 的累计总回报率表明，在这一特定时期，该策略已经产生了经济回报。

缺点是成本。 WEEL 的总费用率为 1.24%，包括收购基金费用和支出，0.25% 的合同费用减免使其目前的净费用率为 0.99%。与传统指数 ETF 相比，这是昂贵的。

也无法保证其近期表现能够持续下去。这个轮子往往会受益于期权溢价足够丰厚且基础资产不会遭受长期崩溃的市场。强大的牛市也可能会抛弃期权销售策略，因为反复将波动性货币化意味着放弃一些上涨空间。

对我来说，这就是权衡。如果我认为美国股票很便宜并且估值倍数将再次持续扩大，我宁愿通过低成本指数 ETF 直接持有它们。然而，按照今天的估值，我可以看到牺牲一些潜在上涨空间以换取大量分配的吸引力。
